summary:
First Flight is a free browser game where you can design, launch, and fly a space mission. You can run missions solo or co-op. 
As Flight Director, you and/or your team must learn to deal with trade-off's as you choose the rocket, orbit, spacecraft, instruments, power, radio, and all features for a space mission while balancing mass, power, budget, data, and communication. In flight, you operate inside your own spacecraft and answer space event anomalies drawn from real NASA space-weather event data. 
The goal is to navigate safely through your mission.

We address the challenge by creating a platform that connects abstract learnings to hands-on experience. 
Our game is designed for students and aspiring engineers who have little opportunity for real-world space experimentation to have a free space where they can run endless missions to success or failure.

Real space missions cost millions of dollars, giving students minimal opportunity to practice in a consequential and collaborative setting. This makes it hard to connect separated and technical learnings to real world application. With our game, we lower the barriers to experimenting in space.
details:
What it does and how it works:

First Flight takes player(s) through a mission of their design in first-person 3D:

1) Briefing:
Player(s) pick a mission (Earth-observing CubeSat, a lunar mapper, a Mars ice radar, or a no-limits Sandbox), read its objective, budget, and science goal.

2) Build:
Walk around mission control and choose the rocket, orbit, spacecraft, instruments, power, battery, radio.
Mass, power, budget, data, communication, schedule update with every choice.
Players must learn to work with the trade-offs of real space missions.

3) Go / No-Go Poll:
Four consoles (plan, spacecraft, science, comms) check their priorities and determine either "Go" or "No-Go" for the mission. One "No-Go" prevents the launch and explains why "No-Go."

4) Launch and Fly:
Walk inside your spacecraft, control time, and answer anomaly cards. Each anomaly comes from real space mission anomalies. Anomalies were collected and chosen from NASA data of space-weather events, furthering consequential weight for players.

5) Debrief:
A score out of 1,000 is given based off design choices and anomaly handling. The mission simulation is rerun for players at the end of the mission, and the reason for success / failure and design changes that could've been made are debriefed to players.

Benefits and Intended Impact:

Students have opportunity and accessibility to experience integrated mission design, which is normally limited to theoretical learnings as real missions are too expensive to practice on.

Failure can become a helpful tool for learning without worldly consequence. Failing missions give helpful debriefs on changes that could've been made, and students can try over and over again.

Teamwork and collaboration within space environments is hard to simulate on Earth, but team play options within our game teach players to negotiate choices in space.

Free, open source, and able to run on any browser makes our game easily accessible.

Technical Tools and Frameworks:

Languages and framworks: TypeScript, React, and Vite

3D: three.js

Multiplayer: PeerJS (WebRTC peer-to-peer) and a small relay endpoint hosted on Vercel

Testing: Vitest (550+ automated tests)

Hosting: GitHub and Vercel

AI Assistance: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor

Creative Aspects:

The anomalies are from NASA space data, meaning they're historical events.

The debrief reruns the simulation to find and suggest fixes instead of only a mission score being shown.

Space immersion as you can actually play from inside the mission with team members or alone.

Factors:

Accuracy: our data is pulled from NASA data and mission designs were created to mimic real ones as best as possible.

Accessibility: free, open source, browser handling, multiple devices.

Learning: our game aims to serve as a platform for curious people to learn freely.
